intro: A playing field is built for a game, but it is never only a game place. A team's employer runs it. A league writes its rules. A city or park district may own the ground. A flag flies over it, and an anthem plays before the first whistle. In this unit you will study what happens when athletes use that crowded space to protest, and when players argue about who gets paid and seen.

The first chapter follows protest on the field, from an Irish jumper on a flagpole in Athens in 1906 to a playoff game that never started in 2020. You will read the First Amendment, two Supreme Court cases about students, and one about a coach. The second chapter follows women's and men's professional sport as two industries, from a wartime baseball league in Rockford, Illinois, to equal-pay contracts signed in 2022.

By the end, you will be able to name the body that wrote a rule, the law that limits it, and the year it changed. You will be able to state a money gap in dollars and explain where the money comes from. And you will practice choosing one frame, such as labor, law or civic life, and using it clearly in an argument.
bigQuestion: When a playing field becomes a place to argue about rights, pay and recognition, whose rules decide what may happen there?

timeline.t: Peter O'Connor climbs a flagpole at the Athens Games to wave an Irish flag
The Star-Spangled Banner is played at the World Series at Comiskey Park, Chicago
Congress makes The Star-Spangled Banner the national anthem
Philip K. Wrigley founds the All-American Girls Professional Baseball League
Thirteen women golfers found the LPGA
Muhammad Ali refuses induction into the U.S. Army
Tommie Smith and John Carlos raise fists on the podium in Mexico City
Tinker v. Des Moines protects students' silent protest at school
The WTA forms in London; Billie Jean King beats Bobby Riggs in Houston
The WNBA plays its first game
Colin Kaepernick sits, then kneels, during the anthem
U.S. Soccer signs equal-pay contracts with the men's and women's teams

words.d: a shared place where citizens gather to speak, argue and be seen
the part of the U.S. Constitution that protects speech, religion, press and assembly from government
the contract a players' union and a league sign about pay, rules and discipline
a refusal to take part in something, used to press for change
a song adopted by a country as its official patriotic song
the Tinker test: a school may limit speech that would seriously interfere with school work
a work stoppage started by workers without formal union approval
a season of events in one sport run by one organization, traveling from place to place
the total money an organizer pays to teams or players at an event
a 1963 U.S. law that bars paying women less than men for equal work
the 1972 federal law barring sex discrimination in education programs that receive federal money
how often and how fully a team or sport is seen in media

test.q: What did Peter O'Connor protest at the 1906 Athens Games?
choices: being listed under Britain instead of Ireland
test.why: O'Connor waved an Irish flag because officials had entered him under Britain.

test.q: Why did Muhammad Ali lose his boxing license in 1967?
choices: He refused induction into the U.S. Army.
test.why: State commissions suspended his license after he refused induction on April 28, 1967.

test.q: Which Chicago ballpark hosted the 1918 World Series game where the anthem was played during the seventh-inning stretch?
test.why: The Cubs played their 1918 Series home games at Comiskey Park.

test.q: Who was IOC president during the 1968 podium protest?
test.why: Avery Brundage, an American from Chicago, led the IOC from 1952 to 1972.

test.q: Why does the First Amendment not directly limit the NFL?
choices: The NFL is a private business, not government.
The NFL plays only on Sundays.
The NFL is run by the IOC.
test.why: The First Amendment limits government; a private league's rules come from contracts.

test.q: Which case said students do not shed their rights at the schoolhouse gate?
test.why: Justice Fortas wrote those words in Tinker v. Des Moines in 1969.

test.q: What did the Milwaukee Bucks do on August 26, 2020?
choices: They refused to take the floor for a playoff game.
test.why: The Bucks stayed in their locker room after police in Kenosha shot Jacob Blake.

test.q: Which U.S. Soccer policy was repealed in June 2020?
choices: equal pay for World Cup games
the policy requiring players to stand for the anthem
test.why: U.S. Soccer adopted a stand-for-the-anthem policy in 2017 and repealed it in 2020.

test.q: What was special about the Rockford Peaches?
choices: They played in the AAGPBL for its whole run, 1943 to 1954.
They were the first WNBA champions.
They won the first Women's World Cup.
test.why: The Rockford Peaches of Illinois played in the AAGPBL from start to finish.

test.q: What did the Original 9 start in 1970?
choices: the women's pro tennis tour that led to the WTA
test.why: Their one-dollar contracts for the Houston event started the Virginia Slims Circuit and, later, the WTA.

test.q: Which Grand Slam paid men and women equally first?
test.why: The U.S. Open paid equal prize money in 1973.

test.q: How much larger was FIFA's 2018 men's prize pool than its 2019 women's pool?
test.why: The 2018 men's pool was 400 million dollars and the 2019 women's pool was 30 million dollars.

test.q: What did the 2022 U.S. Soccer contracts do?
choices: set equal pay and pooled World Cup prize money for both teams
moved the teams to FIFA's control
test.why: The May 2022 agreements set equal pay and split pooled World Cup prize money.

test.q: Which law, signed in 1972, helped build the pipeline of girls' school sports?
test.why: Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972 barred sex discrimination in federally funded schools.

test.q: What did photos from the 2021 NCAA tournaments show?
choices: The women had a larger arena.
The women's weight room was far smaller than the men's.
The men played without fans in Chicago.
test.why: Photos showed one rack of small dumbbells for the women, which led to an outside review.

write.prompt: Pick one protest or one pay dispute from this unit. Was the field a workplace, a public square, or both? Choose one frame and argue from two or three dated documents or records, such as the First Amendment, Tinker (1969), the Equal Pay Act (1963) or FIFA's prize pools.
tips: Name each document or record and its year when you cite it.
Say which body wrote each rule: a league, a federation, a court or Congress.
State money gaps in dollars, not in words like big or small.
Pick one frame, such as labor, law or civic life, and keep it all the way through.
Describe what each side argued before you give your own view.
